title: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from
goal: By the end you can explain why a `System.nanoTime()` loop lies, write a JMH benchmark that returns its result and reads real inputs, and use `-prof gc` to get a number steady enough to trust.
opening:
Picture a restaurant that wants to know which of two cooks makes the house soup faster. The manager hands each cook an order, starts a stopwatch, and stops it when the bowl lands on the counter. Simple enough. But one cook has noticed that nobody ever eats the test bowls, so they stop making them. The stopwatch reads zero.

A loop timed with `System.nanoTime()` gives the JIT the same chance. In this lesson's first demo, a loop of 100 million square roots reported 0.0000 ns per call. The work wasn't fast; it was missing, because nothing used the result.

The trap is easy to fall into, because those numbers look so precise. Lesson 2 asked you to trust a JMH benchmark that counted types at a call site; now JMH has to earn that trust. In this lesson, we'll watch a hand-made timing loop lie, let JMH build the loop instead, learn the two rules that fix most broken benchmarks, and find a number steady enough to check on a busy machine. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: You time 100 million calls of `Math.sqrt(x)` in a loop with `System.nanoTime()` and throw each result away. After a few rounds the loop reports 0.0000 ns per call. What is the best explanation?
options: Your CPU computes square roots in well under a nanosecond
The JIT saw that the results were never used and removed the work from the loop
`System.nanoTime()` is too coarse to measure such short calls
The JVM cached the result of the first call
warmup.why: No CPU does a square root in 0.0000 ns. Once C2 compiled the loop, it proved that nothing used the result of `Math.sqrt(x)` and deleted the call: that's dead-code elimination, the first section's topic. `nanoTime()` is precise enough for a 100-million-lap loop, and the JVM keeps no cache of `Math.sqrt` results.

sections.h: A nanoTime loop measures the optimizer, not your code
sections.body:
Here's the benchmark almost everyone writes first. A **benchmark** is a small program that measures how long some code takes. This one is as simple as it gets: read the clock, call the code many times, read the clock again.

```java
long t0 = System.nanoTime();
for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) {
    Math.sqrt(x);                      // result discarded
}
long t1 = System.nanoTime();
System.out.printf("%.4f ns/op%n", (t1 - t0) / 1e8);
```

```kotlin
val t0 = System.nanoTime()
for (i in 0 until 100_000_000) {
    sqrt(x)                            // result discarded
}
val t1 = System.nanoTime()
println("%.4f ns/op".format((t1 - t0) / 1e8))
```

`NanoLoop`, in the Try it, runs that loop five times, next to a second loop that adds every result to a sum and prints the sum. On JDK 25 it printed (with the sum trimmed off):

```text
round 1: discarded 0.0678 ns/op, used 3.3919 ns/op
round 2: discarded 0.2053 ns/op, used 3.0171 ns/op
round 3: discarded 0.0000 ns/op, used 3.3148 ns/op
round 4: discarded 0.0000 ns/op, used 3.2549 ns/op
round 5: discarded 0.0000 ns/op, used 3.5381 ns/op
```

Zero nanoseconds per square root. That's faster than light, and a little suspicious. The second loop settled at about 3 ns per call, which is believable for a square root and an addition on a busy machine.

The first loop measured nothing because, once C2 had compiled it, there was nothing left to measure. C2 proved that nobody used the result of `Math.sqrt(x)`, so it deleted the call, and then the empty loop. That's **dead-code elimination**: work whose result nobody uses can go. It's the cook skipping the bowl nobody eats.

Here the picture breaks, and in a useful way. A cook who skips a bowl knows they're cutting a corner. The JIT isn't cheating at all. Removing unused work is exactly its job, and our benchmark gave it permission.

Dead code is one of several ways a hand-made loop lies:

- If the input is a constant, C2 can compute the answer at compile time, and you end up timing the load of one number. That's **constant folding**: the cook who gets the same order every time makes it before the doors open.
- The first rounds run in the interpreter and in OSR code, as lesson 1 showed. A benchmark written as one long loop in `main` keeps measuring OSR code.
- The JIT unrolls loops and moves work out of them. JMH's own sample on loops reports the measured cost of an addition falling "up to the point we do each addition with 1/20 ns, well beyond what hardware can actually do".

A broken benchmark can also print a believable number, which is worse. Change the discarded call to `Math.log(x)`. On JDK 21, that loop was never removed: it reported 10 to 13 ns per call, round after round. On JDK 25, it dropped to 0.0000 by round 3, like the square root. Same source, two JDKs, two stories. Whether the JIT can remove a call depends on what it can prove, and you can't see that from the outside.

**A timing loop you wrote by hand measures whatever the JIT left behind. Don't trust its number.**

So we need a loop the JIT can't hollow out, warmed up, in a fresh JVM, timed with care. Writing that by hand is a project of its own. Fortunately, the OpenJDK team already wrote it.

try.title: Watch the work disappear
steps: Read `NanoLoop`. Predict both columns for round 1 and round 5.
Run it. Then run the Kotlin twin.
Change the discarded loop to `Math.log(x)` in either version and run it again. If you have two JDKs installed, try both.

code.title: NanoLoop.java

alt.title: NanoLoop.kt

try.expect: The discarded column starts below 1 ns and reads 0.0000 by round 3; the used column stays near 3 ns. Kotlin does the same. With `Math.log`, the result depends on the JDK: on JDK 21 the discarded loop reported 10 to 13 ns per call and never reached zero, while on JDK 25 it reached 0.0000 by round 3. Neither loop tells you the real cost of the method.

try.title: Five ways to measure one square root
steps: Read `TrapsBench`. Predict which of the five benchmarks will score about the same as `baseline`.
Run it (under 10 seconds). Then run the Kotlin twin, which runs two of the five with JMH's full output, so you can watch the warm-up and measurement iterations go by.
Change `double x = 2.0;` to `final double x = 2.0;` and run the Java version again. Which benchmarks change?

code.title: TrapsBench.java

alt.title: TrapsBench.kt

try.expect: `sqrtDiscarded` and `sqrtOfConstant` land on top of `baseline`, between 0.4 and 0.9 ns on the busy course machine. `sqrtReturned` and `sqrtBlackhole` take about 2 to 5 ns. With `final double x = 2.0`, javac copies `2.0` into every method, so every benchmark drops to the baseline, `sqrtReturned` and `sqrtBlackhole` included: 0.44 and 0.47 ns in the run here. The Kotlin twin's log shows `# Blackhole mode: compiler (auto-detected ...)` and ends with JMH's "REMEMBER: The numbers below are just data" warning.

sections.h: Two rules: consume every result, read inputs from non-final fields
Count bytes with -prof gc, because they don't wobble

try.title: Count the bytes
steps: Predict the B/op of each benchmark in `WordCountBench`, roughly.
Run it (about 7 seconds). Compare the error columns for time and for bytes.
Run the Kotlin twin. It writes the same two counts in Kotlin and counts bytes with the JVM's per-thread allocation counter instead of JMH. Why might its `split` number differ from Java's?

code.title: WordCountBench.java

alt.title: WordCountBench.kt

try.expect: `wordsBySplit` allocates about 54,400 bytes per call with a small error, while its time error is huge on a busy machine. `wordsByScan` allocates almost nothing (under 1 byte, which is JMH's own rounding). The Kotlin twin prints exactly 56000.000 and 0.000 B/op. Kotlin's `split` is a different function from Java's: it returns a `List` of new strings, not an array, so its count is a little higher. The scan allocates nothing in either language.

compare.title: Constants that get baked into the bytecode

java.title: Java

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.src:
const val WORDS_PER_MINUTE = 238L               // copied by kotlinc; WORDS_PER_MINUTE * 2 becomes 476

open class Inputs(val fromCtor: Long) {         // a real field read
    val words = 1_234L                          // NOT copied: kotlinc reads the field
    var plain = 1_234L                          // what a benchmark input should be
}

compare.note: Java copies any `final` field with a constant initializer into the code that uses it, instance fields included. Kotlin copies only `const val`. A Kotlin `val words = 1_234L` compiles to a `getfield`, as `javap` shows, so kotlinc doesn't fold it. Use `var` in a Kotlin benchmark anyway, because it tells the next reader "this is an input". Both compilers also do arithmetic on constants themselves: in Kotlin, `WORDS_PER_MINUTE * 2` compiled to `ldc2_w 476`. In either language, a benchmark that reads only constants measures the JIT's arithmetic, not yours.

worked.title: Turn a nanoTime test into a benchmark you can trust

steps.say: A pull request (a proposed change, waiting for review) claims the new word counter is "3x faster", based on this test. Spot the problems before reading on.

Four problems. The results are dropped (dead code). The input is a constant (folding). The first loop warms up the JVM, so the second inherits a warm JVM and a mixed profile. And a timing assertion in a unit test fails at random on a busy build machine. Move the comparison to JMH, with the input in a non-final field.

Add a `@Param` so the input isn't one magic line, and turn on `-prof gc` so you get a steady second number. Self-check: why does `@Param` take strings? (Answer: JMH sets the field from text, one run per value, so the values also show up in the results table.)
steps.code:
@Param({"a", "the quick report", "a much longer line with many more words in it"})
String line;
steps.alt_code:
@Param("a", "the quick report", "a much longer line with many more words in it")
var line = ""

steps.say: Read the result with the error column, and check the baseline first. If `newCounter` sits on the baseline, it measures nothing. If the error bars of the two counters overlap, "3x faster" isn't proven. And if `newCounter` allocates 0 B/op where `oldCounter` allocates 160, that's a result you can put in the pull request whatever the timer says.
steps.code:
Benchmark                              (line)  Mode  Cnt   Score   Error   Units
CounterBench.newCounter                    ...  avgt   15   ...     ...   ns/op
CounterBench.newCounter:gc.alloc.rate.norm ...  avgt   15   ...     ...    B/op

lab.title: Fix three broken benchmarks
steps: The three benchmarks measure the report service's `ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words)`, the reading time from lesson 1. Run the tests. Five of six fail; the sixth only checks that the classes are still JMH benchmarks. The tests never time anything: they call your benchmark methods and inspect them with reflection.
`DeadResultBench`: make `seconds()` hand its result to JMH.
`ConstantInputBench`: make `words` an input the compiler can't know. Keep the field name, because the test sets it to other values and expects `seconds()` to follow.

`ColdBatchBench`: move building the batch into a `@Setup` method that runs once per fork, and keep only the adding up in `totalSeconds()`. Then give it real warm-up (at least 3 iterations) and at least one fork.
Run the tests until all six pass. Optional: copy one fixed class into `src/demo/.../l03`, give it a `main` like `TrapsBench`'s, and run it before and after your fix.
hints: For `DeadResultBench`, changing `void` to `long` and adding `return` is the whole fix. A `Blackhole` parameter also passes, but one result reads better as a return value.
For `ConstantInputBench`, look at `javap -c -p` on the compiled class before and after. Before: `ldc2_w 1234`. After: `getfield words`.

In `ColdBatchBench`, add a `long[] batch` field and a `@Setup(Level.Trial) public void buildBatch()` method. Don't use `Level.Invocation`: it runs setup around every single call and distorts short benchmarks.
`@Fork(0)` runs the benchmark inside the JVM that launched it, with that JVM's profile and garbage. Use at least 1, ideally 2 or more.

drill.title: Write a correct benchmark from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a JMH benchmark that measures `ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words)` over a 1,000-document batch built by `Fixtures.batch(1000)`. Include the state, setup, warm-up, measurement, forks and mode. Then check it against the answer: is the batch built outside the measurement, is the result consumed, and are the inputs non-final fields?

recap: A hand-made `nanoTime` loop measures the optimizer: dead code is removed (0.0000 ns/op), constants are folded, the first rounds run cold, and loops get unrolled. Whether a call disappears can even change between JDKs.
JMH generates the measuring loop, runs warm-up iterations it throws away, then measurement iterations in fresh JVMs (`@Fork`), and reports a score with an error.
Return every result or `consume` it in a `Blackhole`, and read inputs from non-final `@State` fields. Java copies a `final` field with a constant initializer straight into your method.
Compare against an empty `baseline()` benchmark: anything that scores like it is measuring nothing.
`-prof gc` gives `gc.alloc.rate.norm`, bytes per operation. It stays steady on a busy machine, so it's the number to check in CI; time isn't.
The limit: a benchmark measures a small piece of code on its own, usually on one thread. It can't tell you which piece of a real program is slow; that's the profilers' job in lessons 5 and 6.
closing:
We started with a cook who stops making the test bowls nobody eats, and a stopwatch that reads zero. A `nanoTime` loop invites the JIT to do the same. JMH runs the fair taste test instead: a warmed-up kitchen, a fresh one for each fork, unpredictable ingredients in `@State` fields, and a judge who eats every result.

Now search your own tests for `System.nanoTime()` next to an `assert`. Each one is a timing check that will fail at random on a busy build machine, or a benchmark that measured less than it claims.

Next, we'll leave the single thread behind: why can two threads that never touch the same field still slow each other down?

quiz.q: A benchmark method is `public void seconds() { ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words); }`. It scores 0.6 ns/op, the same as an empty benchmark. What is the most likely reason?
options: The reading-time calculation really takes 0.6 ns
The result is discarded, so the JIT removed the calculation
JMH's timer can't resolve anything under 1 ns
The benchmark didn't fork
quiz.why: A result nobody uses is dead code, and C2 deletes it. Return the value (JMH consumes return values) or pass it to a `Blackhole`. Matching the empty baseline is the giveaway.

quiz.q: Which input declaration lets C2 fold `ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words)` into a constant in a Java benchmark?
options: `long words = 1_234;` in the `@State` class
`@Param("1234") long words;`
`private final long words = 1_234;`
`long words;` assigned in a `@Setup` method
quiz.why: A `final` field with a constant initializer is a compile-time constant in Java, so javac writes `ldc2_w 1234` into the method and C2 can compute the result once. The other three are real field reads that C2 can't predict.

quiz.q: You must compare two word counters in CI and fail the build when the new one gets worse. Which JMH number should the check use?
options: The ns/op score
The error column
The number of warm-up iterations
`gc.alloc.rate.norm` (bytes per operation)
quiz.why: Allocation per operation is the same every time for the same code and input, so its error is tiny. Time on a shared build machine has error bars that can be bigger than the score, so a time threshold fails at random.

quiz.q: A colleague's benchmark uses `@Fork(0)` "to make it faster to run". What do they lose?
options: A fresh JVM: the benchmark now shares the launcher's profile, heap and JIT state, so code that ran earlier can change its result
Nothing, forks only matter for benchmarks with several threads
The warm-up iterations
The ability to use `@Setup`
quiz.why: With 0 forks, the benchmark runs inside the JVM that started JMH. Its type profiles and compiled code are shared with whatever ran before, as lesson 2's `MegamorphicBench` showed by running each case in its own fork.

quiz.q: From lesson 2: `MegamorphicBench` ran each `@Param` value (1, 2 and 3 types) in its own fork. What would likely happen to the 1-type result if all three ran in the same JVM, 3 types first?
options: Nothing, each @Param value gets fresh compiled code
The 1-type case would likely look slow too, because the call site's profile already holds three types
It would get faster, because the JIT is already warm
JMH would refuse to run
quiz.why: The type profile belongs to the call site in the bytecode, not to the @Param value, and it keeps counting from start-up. After three types have been seen there, C2 compiles a virtual call, and the 1-type run inherits it. Forks give every case a clean profile.

flashcards.front: Why did a `nanoTime` loop around a discarded `Math.sqrt(x)` report 0.0000 ns/op?
flashcards.back: Dead-code elimination: C2 proved the result was unused and removed the call.

flashcards.front: How do you make sure JMH can't throw a benchmark's result away?
flashcards.back: Return it from the `@Benchmark` method, or pass it to `Blackhole.consume` when there are several results.

flashcards.front: Why must JMH inputs be non-final `@State` fields?
flashcards.back: A `final` field with a constant initializer is copied into the method by javac (and `static final` values are known to the JIT), so C2 can fold the computation.
Two fresh JVMs per benchmark, each with a clean profile and heap. `@Fork(0)` runs in the launcher's JVM.

flashcards.front: What does `gc.alloc.rate.norm` measure, and why is it useful in CI?
flashcards.back: Bytes allocated per benchmark operation (`-prof gc`). It's the same every run for the same code and input, so its error is near zero.

flashcards.front: In Kotlin, which property is copied into callers as a constant: `val x = 5L` or `const val X = 5L`?
flashcards.back: Only `const val`. A plain `val` in a class compiles to a field read.

flashcards.front: What is a baseline benchmark for?
flashcards.back: An empty `@Benchmark` method measures the harness alone. Any benchmark that scores like it is measuring nothing.

terms.plain: A small program that measures how long some code takes.
The JIT removing work whose result nothing uses.
Computing a result at compile time because the inputs are known constants.
The Java Microbenchmark Harness: generates and runs correct measuring loops.
A JMH class whose fields hold benchmark inputs, with a scope such as one instance per thread.
A fresh JVM that JMH starts to run a benchmark in.
A JMH object that consumes values so the JIT must compute them.
Bytes allocated per operation, reported by JMH's GC profiler.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate pastes "new word counter: 12 ns/op, old one: 40 ns/op" from a loop timed with `System.nanoTime()`. Explain, in your own words, why you don't trust it yet and what you'd ask for instead.
explain_back.answer: A hand-made loop measures whatever the JIT left behind. If the counter's result isn't used, C2 can delete the work. If the input is a constant, it can fold it. And the first loop runs partly in the interpreter, while the second runs in a warmed-up JVM with a profile the first one shaped. So 12 against 40 might measure dead code, warm-up order or OSR. I'd ask for a JMH benchmark with the input text in a non-final @State field, the count returned, an empty baseline to compare with, a few forks so each run gets a fresh JVM, and `-prof gc` so we also get bytes per operation. That number is steady enough to trust and to check in CI.

deeper.body:
Three more JMH features are worth knowing before you need them.

`@State(Scope.Benchmark)` shares one state object across all benchmark threads, and `@Threads(4)` or `@Group` runs several threads at once. That's how you measure contention, threads getting in each other's way: for example 4 threads incrementing one `AtomicLong` against one `LongAdder`. Lesson 4 talks about why those differ.

`Mode.SampleTime` records the times of individual calls and prints percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9), which fits questions about slow requests better than an average does. `Mode.SingleShotTime` measures one call per iteration, which suits questions about cold starts.

JMH pads `@State` objects automatically against one kind of interference between threads: the JMH false-sharing sample says "@States are automatically padded", but "This padding does not extend to the State internals". Fields inside your state object can still share a cache line, which is lesson 4's topic.

If you want to see what C2 really did to a benchmark, `-prof perfasm` prints the busiest generated machine code next to the hardware counters. It needs Linux `perf` and the hsdis disassembler. Without it, the cheap check is the one you already know: put an empty baseline next to every benchmark, and be suspicious of anything that scores like it.
